title: Finite-energy two-way assisted capacities: Exact formulas for multimode loss and fading
abstract: We study quantum communication, entanglement distribution, and secret-key generation through multimode bosonic loss and fading channels, assisted by local quantum operations and two-way classical communication. Using sector teleportation, we determine the exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities of multimode pure-loss channels under a mean photon-number constraint, allowing arbitrary adaptive quantum protocols. We extend these results to continuous frequency-dependent loss under a power constraint and identify the optimal allocation of photons among optical modes. For constant loss over an unlimited bandwidth, we obtain a closed-form capacity proportional to the square root of power. For randomly varying loss, we determine exact finite-energy capacities when the channel realization is publicly revealed, distinguishing knowledge before and after transmission. When fading remains unobserved, we derive capacity bounds and explicit formulas for an on/off channel. We also establish strong-converse bounds, with exact thresholds for the deterministic loss models considered here, observed fading, and unobserved fading with finitely many possible transmissivities. Under mean energy constraints, these thresholds generally exceed the corresponding finite-energy capacities. These results guide energy allocation and provide benchmarks for energy-constrained optical quantum communication with multimode signals and variable loss.
summary: This paper derives exact formulas for the fundamental capacities (quantum, entanglement, private, and key) achievable in quantum communication over lossy, multimode channels. By imposing finite-energy constraints, the authors show that these different capacities are equal and provide explicit rules for optimally allocating limited photon resources across different spectral modes. This work is vital for advancing the theory and engineering of energy-efficient quantum optical communication systems.
main_problem: The paper determines the exact two-way quantum and secret-key capacities for quantum communication tasks over multimode bosonic loss and fading channels.
main_result: The authors establish that under finite-energy constraints, the quantum, entanglement, private, and secret-key capacities all coincide, yielding closed-form expressions dependent on the channel loss and energy budget.
method: The analysis employs techniques like sector teleportation, finite-energy converse arguments, and optimization calculus (Lagrange multipliers) to find the optimal photon allocation across multiple modes.
model_or_system: The system models quantum communication through multimode bosonic loss and fading channels, which can be extended to continuous frequency-dependent loss under a power constraint.
key_observables: Two-way quantum capacity ($Q_2$), entanglement distribution capacity ($D_2$), private capacity ($P_2$), and secret-key capacity ($K_2$).
important_parameters: Mean photon-number constraint ($N$) or mean input power ($P$); channel transmissivities ($\eta_j$ or $\eta(\omega)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the availability of local quantum operations and two-way classical communication, and it distinguishes between observed and unobserved fading realizations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a three-mode example comparing the exact capacity against two feasible allocations and the derived optimal allocation.
paper_structure: The paper builds from discrete multimode loss channels to continuous frequency-dependent loss, establishing capacity identities ($Q_2=D_2=P_2=K_2$) and deriving optimal energy allocation rules for both finite and continuous settings.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, energy-constrained benchmarks for quantum communication protocols, which is crucial for designing practical quantum networks using optical fiber or free-space links where loss and fading are inevitable.

FIG. 4. Structure of the proof. The single-mode block estimate (lemma 1) yields the adaptive replica and finite-list bounds (lemmas 3 and 5). Scalar duality and spectral tail estimates turn these into the continuum converse. The sector resource (lemma 2) supplies finite-dimensional hashing, first for discrete modes and then for spectral intervals. Together these branches prove theorem 4. Evaluating the flat-profile integral gives theorem 5. The threshold statements also use the unconstrained resource comparison and public vacuum randomization, as detailed in Appendices E and I.
